t.7.36.1: Then, seeing the Grandfather, Vāyu the sustainer, tormented by the slaying of his son, took up that little child and rose up before him.
t.7.36.2: Vāyu, adorned with swaying earrings, a diadem, a garland and ornaments of gold, three times stood up and fell at the feet of the Creator.
t.7.36.3: Then the foremost of the knowers of the Veda raised up Vāyu, and with his hand, resplendent with hanging ornaments, he gently stroked that child.
t.7.36.4: Then, as soon as he was touched with playful ease by the Lotus-born, he regained his life, like a crop sprinkled with water.
t.7.36.5: Seeing him alive once more, the Wind, the life-breath and bearer of fragrance, joyfully moved again among all beings as before, and what had been held back flowed freely once more.
t.7.36.6: Freed from the affliction caused by the wind, the creatures indeed became joyful, like lotus ponds with their lotuses freed from the cold wind.
t.7.36.7: Then Brahmā, possessor of the three pairs, the three-peaked one of threefold abode, worshipped by the thirty gods, spoke to the deities out of a desire to please Māruta.
t.7.36.8: O Mahendra, Agni, Varuṇa, Dhaneśvara and Maheśvara! Let all of you know this as well: I shall declare all that is beneficial; let it be heard.
t.7.36.9: A task of yours that must be done will be accomplished by this child. All of you, grant him boons that will bring satisfaction to this Māruta.
t.7.36.10: Then the thousand-eyed one, his fair face flushed with affection, lifted up a garland made of lotuses and spoke these words.
t.7.36.11: Since his jaw was struck by the thunderbolt released from my hand, this tiger among monkeys shall be known by the name Hanumān.
t.7.36.12: I myself will grant him a supreme and excellent boon: from this time forth he shall not be slain by my vajra.
t.7.36.13: Then the blessed Mārtāṇḍa, dispeller of darkness, spoke there: "I give a hundredth portion of this radiance of mine."
t.7.36.14: But when he has the capacity to study the treatises, then I shall give him a treatise by which he will become eloquent.
t.7.36.15: And Varuṇa granted a boon: "Not even in a hundred times ten thousand years shall his death come from my noose or from water."
t.7.36.16: Yama too, well pleased, granted him as a boon immunity from his rod of punishment, constant freedom from disease, and freedom from despondency in battle.
t.7.36.17: "This mace of mine shall not slay him in battles": thus then spoke the boon-giving Ekākṣipiṅgala, the one with a single tawny eye.
t.7.36.18: "He shall not be slain by me or by my weapons": thus Śaṃkara too granted him a supreme boon.
t.7.36.19: "He shall be beyond the reach of every brahmadaṇḍa, the rod of Brahmā, and shall be long-lived and great-souled": thus did Brahmā speak these words.
t.7.36.20: Then Viśvakarmā, the foremost of craftsmen and great of mind, seeing this child who resembled the rising sun, spoke a boon for him.
t.7.36.21: Whatever weapons have been fashioned here for the gods, by those he shall not be slain in the time of battle.
t.7.36.22: Then, seeing him adorned with the boons of the gods, the four-faced one, the preceptor of the world, his face beaming with satisfaction, spoke to Vāyu.
t.7.36.23: O Māruta, your son Māruti will be a source of fear to his enemies and a giver of fearlessness to his friends; here he will be invincible.
t.7.36.24: In battle he will perform deeds that aim at the destruction of Rāvaṇa, that bring delight to Rāma, and that make the hair stand on end.
t.7.36.25: Having spoken thus and taken leave of Māruta, they all, with the Grandfather at their head, went back together with the immortals by the way they had come.
t.7.36.26: The Wind-god, bearer of fragrance, took his son and brought him home; and having told Añjanā of the boon that had been granted, he went forth.
t.7.36.27: Having obtained these boons, O Rāma, he, endowed with the power that the granting of boons bestows, was filled with the strength abiding within himself, just as the ocean is filled.
t.7.36.28: For this bull among monkeys, being filled with strength, fearlessly commits offences in the hermitages of the great sages.
t.7.36.29: This one smashes, tears apart and wrecks the sacrificial ladles and vessels, the agnihotra, and the heaps of bark garments belonging to the deeply tranquil sages.
t.7.36.30: Knowing that he had been made by Brahmā invulnerable to all brahmadaṇḍas, the ṛṣis always forgive him his misdeeds.
t.7.36.31: When this monkey, though restrained by Kesarin and by Vāyu together with Añjana, still kept overstepping the bounds of propriety.
t.7.36.32: Then, O best of the Raghus, the great sages born in the lines of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras, though angered, cursed him, yet without excessive anger or wrath.
t.7.36.33: Since you torment us, O monkey, relying on your strength, you will not know that strength for a long time, deluded by our curse.
t.7.36.34: Then, his splendor and vigor taken away by the power of the great sages' words, he no longer trespasses upon the hermitages, but roams about having become gentle in nature.
t.7.36.35: Now Ṛkṣarajas by name, the father of Vālin and Sugrīva, was king of all the monkeys, like the sun in his splendour.
t.7.36.36: That lord of the monkeys named Ṛkṣarajas, having ruled the kingdom of the vānaras for a long time, then passed away through his union with the law of Time.
t.7.36.37: When he had passed away, Vālī was made king in his father's place by ministers skilled in counsel, and Sugrīva was installed in Vālī's former place.
t.7.36.38: His friendship with Sugrīva was undivided, free of any flaw, and unshakable, like that of the wind with fire.
t.7.36.39: Solely because of the curse, this one did not know his own strength when the enmity between Vālin and Sugrīva arose, O Rāma.
t.7.36.40: For, O Rāma, even while Sugrīva was being driven about by Vālin, he did not know of it, nor indeed was Māruti himself aware of the strength within him.
t.7.36.41: In valour, zeal, intelligence and majesty, in good character, sweetness and the discernment of sound and unsound policy, in depth, skill, great prowess and steadfastness, who in the world is superior to Hanūmān?
t.7.36.42: Long ago, wishing to learn grammar, this lord of monkeys, his face turned toward Sūrya and following close behind him, went from the mountain of sunrise to the mountain of sunset; and that immeasurable one retained in memory a great text.
t.7.36.43: Who will stand before Hanumān, who is like the ocean longing to sweep into the worlds, like fire longing to burn them up, like Antaka at the dissolutions of the worlds?
t.7.36.45: All this that you ask of me has now been told. This deed of Hanumān in his childhood has been narrated by me.
t.7.36.44: This one too, and the other great lords of the monkeys, Sugrīva, Mainda and Dvivida, together with Nīla, with Tāra, Tāreya and Nala, and with Rambha, were indeed created by the gods for your sake, O Rāma.
t.7.36.46: "You have been seen and spoken with, Rāma; we shall now depart." Having spoken thus, all those sages went back the way they had come.
